rashi:a3.1: Make a protection for it: as it is written, “the charge [mishmeret]”.
rashi:a4.1: Once he spread his garment over her: that the master designated the Hebrew maidservant [as his wife], married her and spread his wings over her. The father may no longer sell her, even if the master divorced her, since a man does not sell his daughter into servitude after marriage. And we have established in the first chapter of Kiddushin (18b) that Rabbi Eliezer holds that the spelling is authoritative: “bevigdo bah” is written without a yod, and that is the language of deceit [begida], like other words written without a yod that you read with a ḥataf kamatz, as in “kishmo’o” (Genesis 39).
rashi:a5.1: Since he dealt deceitfully with her: her father, who sold her into servitude, may no longer sell her, since a man does not sell his daughter into servitude after servitude; but after marriage he may sell her. And they say there [in Kiddushin] that Rabbi Akiva holds that the vocalization is authoritative: we read “bevigdo” [his garment]. Some corrupt the passage in tractate Kiddushin and read: Rabbi Eliezer holds that the vocalization is authoritative and Rabbi Akiva holds that the spelling is authoritative. But they are in error, for if so, what is the difficulty raised here in Bekhorot?
rashi:a7.1: Rabbi Shimon: who says in the mishna, “One may let the blood even though it causes a blemish,” and does not say that one may slaughter on account of it.
rashi:a8.1: The halakha is in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda: in tractate Shabbat (22a), who says that an unintentional act is prohibited.
rashi:a8.2: The halakha is in accordance with Rabbi Shimon: so why would he need to teach it again here?
rashi:a8.3: Without men: without Rav Ḥiyya and Rav Ḥanan [Rashi writes “Rav Ḥanan”, where the Davidson English here has Rav Ḥanin bar Ashi].
rashi:a9.1: Of the baraita: who says that one may even slaughter on account of that blemish. Since his intention was not to cause a blemish in order to permit it, but so that it would not die, we do not penalize him.
rashi:a10.1: Mishna. One who slits: who damages it (Rashi adds an Old French gloss). And it is speaking of a priest.
rashi:a11.1: Gemara. But does Rabbi Eliezer penalize forever: that it will never be permitted?
tosafot:a1.1: Both a blemish and any blemish: even those tanna’im who do not expound “any [kol]”, in the chapter Elu Overin (Pesaḥim 43b), may expound it here, since there is a reason for it, as explained there.
tosafot:a3.1: One teruma that is pure and one teruma that is in abeyance: And if you say: in the chapter Bameh Madlikin (Shabbat 25a) we say “and one that is impure, and the Merciful One said: it shall be yours, for kindling under your cooked dish.” How, then, do three terumot emerge from the verse: pure, impure and in abeyance? One can say: since it is written “I have given you the charge of My terumot,” “My terumot” relates both to “you” and to “charge.” “You” relates to the impure teruma, to include it as permitted for benefit, and “charge” relates to the teruma in abeyance, which requires safeguarding.
tosafot:a3.2: And Rabbi Yehoshua: “terumati” is written: And if you say: according to Rabbi Yehoshua, since the verse does not speak of two terumot, from where does he know that impure teruma is permitted for benefit? One can say that he derives it from the other expositions there, in the chapter Bameh Madlikin (ibid.): “From it you may not kindle…”, or “…but not for its light,” which implies that it is [otherwise] fit for its light [the wording here is abbreviated in the text].
tosafot:a4.1: In brief: Rashi’s text reads “once he spread his garment over her, he may no longer sell her” as the statement of Rabbi Akiva, and “since he dealt deceitfully with her” as Rabbi Eliezer’s, and in the first chapter of Kiddushin (18b) Rashi brings proof from the Mekhilta, which has “once he spread his garment” in Rabbi Akiva’s words and does not have Rabbi Eliezer’s at all. But most old manuscripts read the reverse, here and in Kiddushin (ibid.). Further: Rashi’s reading puts Rabbi Akiva’s words before those of Rabbi Eliezer, who was his teacher; most texts repeat “bevigdo bah, bevigdo bah” twice before “once he spread his garment”; and how would Rabbi Eliezer get “deceit” from the spelling without a yod, when it is not written with a vav either? Though without a vav one reads a ḥataf kamatz, as Rashi explained (kishmo’o, kishmo’am, be’omram, ke’ovram), so too, if it meant garment, one would not ordinarily write a yod in the middle of such a form. Also, in the nearby passage in Kiddushin all the old texts read that Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak, who says the first money was given for betrothal, establishes it according to Rabbi Akiva, who says one cannot sell her into servitude after servitude but can after marriage; on Rashi’s reading one would have to emend this to Rabbi Eliezer. Rabbeinu Tam therefore reads: “Once he spread his garment over her…”: the statement of Rabbi Eliezer; Rabbi Akiva says: “Once he dealt deceitfully with her.” Then it is the vocalization that means deceit, for if it meant garment we would read “bevigdo” with a tzeirei (and although we read “vatitpesehu bevigdo,” Genesis 39:12, here is different, because one might err); and the spelling without a yod suggests garment more than deceit. That is why the baraita says “bevigdo” twice: you should have written it with a yod so as not to err, yet it is written without a yod to say “once he spread his garment…”. In the Mekhilta that has “spread his garment” in Rabbi Akiva’s words, the scribe left out Rabbi Eliezer and all of Rabbi Akiva’s own statement; and in Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak’s passage one reads “establishes it according to Rabbi Akiva,” as all the old texts have it. A slight difficulty remains: in Kiddushin the Gemara asks, “But if her father betrothed her, can he sell her? A man does not sell his daughter into servitude after marriage,” even though, on this reading, that is the view of Rabbi Eliezer, who is a Shammaite. One can say it is obvious to us that this is the halakha, because the Rabbis who disagree with Rabbi Shimon there, and Rabbi Shimon himself, agree with him and say: but not into servitude after marriage. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:a7.1: In brief: If we say it is Rabbi Shimon of the mishna, hasn’t Shmuel already taught us that an unintentional act is permitted? This is puzzling: does Rabbi Shimon permit because the act is unintentional? He permits even where it is impossible not to cause a blemish, which is causing a blemish intentionally, since it was said above that they disagree about verses, and he permits because it is written “It shall be perfect to be accepted” (Leviticus 22:21): one who causes a blemish in an already blemished animal is permitted; and in the chapter Kol HaMenaḥot Ba’ot Matza (Menaḥot 56b) their reasons are likewise explained from verses. On Rashi’s explanation earlier, in the chapter HaLoke’aḥ Behema (25a), of the two hairs of a cow whose roots are red and tips black, where Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam says one may shear them with scissors without concern, Rashi explained that it counts as unintentional, since he intends not to shear but to fix the cow. On that view this passage works well too: here it is unintentional with regard to the blemish, being only for healing, so the Gemara asks why Shmuel needed to rule like Rabbi Shimon, since even if one prohibited causing a blemish in a blemished animal it would be permitted here as healing, and Shmuel already holds that an unintentional act is permitted. But Rashi’s explanation cannot stand, as explained there. Better to explain that there are two disputes. In the baraita they disagree about causing a blemish in an animal already blemished: one so congested with blood that it cannot be healed without bloodletting and would die, which counts as a blemish; and even if it would not die, since it would never be free of the congestion unless one let blood where it causes a blemish, it counts as blemished. Rabbi Meir prohibits letting blood where it causes a blemish, since he holds “there shall be no blemish in it” applies even to a blemished animal; the Rabbis permit, because of “It shall be perfect to be accepted,” but not slaughtering on account of that blemish, as a decree lest one do so where it would not die without a blemish, and counts as unblemished, or where it could be healed by letting blood where no blemish results; Rabbi Shimon permits even slaughtering, as he does not decree; and Rabbi Yehuda prohibits even where no blemish results, as explained in the first chapter of Pesaḥim (11b): since a person is anxious about his money, if you permit it where no blemish results he will come to do it where one does. In the mishna the dispute is different: Rabbi Yehuda says one may not let the blood in any way, even if it would die; the Rabbis say one may, whether or not it would die, provided one takes care not to cause a blemish, for example near the ear, the lips or the nose, since they hold that an unintentional act is prohibited, and where it would not die it does not count as blemished; Rabbi Shimon says one may let blood even though it may lead to a blemish, since an unintentional act is permitted. The wording of the mishna suggests this, since it does not speak of a place that causes a blemish and a place that does not, as the baraita does. And if you ask: since congestion that cannot be healed without a blemish counts as a blemish, let one slaughter on account of it? It is prohibited by rabbinic law, lest it be confused with an unblemished animal; or it counts as a passing blemish that has a cure. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:a11.1: But does Rabbi Eliezer penalize forever? And the Gemara raises a contradiction: one who had…: Several passages prove that the ruling on one who slits the ear of a firstborn is a penalty, and just below too it says: “with this blemish the Rabbis penalized him.” And even according to Rava, who says in the first chapter of Temura (4b) that whatever the Merciful One said not to do, if one does it, it is ineffective, here the firstborn is permitted by Torah law, since it has a blemish, and this man is pure, since he has no leprous mark at all. And if you say: in the Sifrei, on the portion Re’eh, it is taught: Rabbi Eliezer says… one who causes a blemish in a firstborn and eats it transgresses, as it is said: “You shall not eat any abomination” (Deuteronomy 14:3); evidently it is prohibited by Torah law? One can say: just below we find this penalty according to the Rabbis, who hold like the Aḥerim, who expound that verse there as speaking of disqualified consecrated animals or of cooking meat in milk, as stated in the chapter Kol HaBasar (Ḥullin 114b); and one cannot prohibit slaughtering on account of that blemish from “You shall not eat any abomination,” as with meat in milk, diverse kinds of seeds and work done on Shabbat, for one can distinguish. And if you say: according to Rabbi Eliezer, who does not make that distinction, what is the challenge from the baheret? One who slits the ear of a firstborn is prohibited by Torah law until another blemish develops, so we should penalize him when another blemish develops; whereas one who excises a baheret is pure by Torah law as soon as it is excised, [and is penalized only] until another mark develops. One can say: even so, we should not have penalized him forever with the blemish, but only until a third or fourth blemish. Alternatively: granted that if Rabbi Eliezer permitted slaughter for another blemish there would be no penalty here at all, still we should not penalize him with a blemish through which he committed no transgression, just as he does not penalize him with another leprous mark. Alternatively, the Sifrei is a mere supporting allusion [asmakhta].
gershom:a1.1: It says “blemish”, for one caused by direct action, and it says “any blemish”, that he should not cause one [indirectly].
gershom:a2.1: And Rabbi Yehoshua holds “terumati” is written: that is, teruma that is pure requires safeguarding, but not teruma in abeyance.
gershom:a3.1: That Rabbi Eliezer holds the vocalization is authoritative: as we read it, “terumotai.”
gershom:a4.1: And the Gemara raises a contradiction: “bevigdo bah.” [An editor’s footnote here says that Rabbeinu Gershom’s reading is like that of Tosafot, in the comment beginning “Ilema”.] Once he spread his garment over her for designation, he may no longer sell her. Evidently he follows the spelling, since the plain sense of the verse is the language of deceit, that is: since he dealt deceitfully with her by selling her once, he may no longer sell her.
gershom:a5.1: And Rabbi Eliezer expounds according to the spelling, as the language of a garment, a cloak; for if it were as its plain sense, it would have been enough to say “bevaged bah.” Since “bevigdo” is written, that is “garment.” And this is difficult for what we learn in tractate Kiddushin, where it says: “In what do they disagree? Rabbi Eliezer holds that the vocalization is authoritative.” Another version, in the name of Rabbi Yitzḥak the Elder, of blessed memory: “Once he dealt deceitfully with her, her father no longer has authority over her; the statement of Rabbi Eliezer.” Evidently he holds that the spelling is authoritative, according to what is written, “bevagdo,” and not as we read it, “bevigdo.” And it is also difficult for that passage in Kiddushin, where Rabbi Eliezer said “once he spread his cloak” and it says that the vocalization is authoritative. Rather, they disagree about “you”: “And I, behold, I have given you.” [The text of this comment is difficult; we have rendered it as it stands.]
gershom:a6.1: That which is fit for you: which is pure, safeguard.
gershom:a7.1: The halakha is in accordance with Rabbi Shimon: of the baraita, who says one may even slaughter on account of that blemish. The reason of Rabban Gamliel, who said “one should do nothing new with it,” is like that of Rabbi Eliezer: lest Elijah come and deem them pure.
gershom:a8.1: One who slits: who damages it intentionally may never slaughter it, since we penalize him.
gershom:a9.1: And the Rabbis say: he may not slaughter on account of this blemish, but when another blemish develops in it, he may slaughter on account of that one.
rashi:b1.1: And it got excised: he did not intend to excise it.
rashi:b1.2: When he will develop another leprous mark: for now he is impure and afflicted [by this new mark].
rashi:b1.3: He will become pure: from the first one. We follow this one, and if he is healed of it, he is pure of them all, since it has become clear that the first one too would have healed like this one.
rashi:b2.1: Until it spreads over all of him: the latter mark. Then there is nothing to be concerned about, since even if the first mark were on him it would now be pure, as it is written: “And if the leprosy cover all the skin of him that has the plague” (Leviticus 13:12).
rashi:b2.2: Or until his baheret shrinks: the first one, to less than a split bean, before he excised it. But if at the time he excised it, it was the size of a leprous mark, he has no purification ever, since we penalize him forever.
rashi:b4.1: With his property he might come to do it: either way. He thinks: I will cause a blemish in it, and if they permit it to me on account of this, I have gained; and if not, what have I lost? If I wait for another blemish, I would have waited for a blemish to develop anyway. Therefore we penalize him even if another blemish develops in it, so that he will not come to do it.
rashi:b4.2: With his body, is there reason to say: that he would leave the doubt as it is and excise it, if we did not penalize him forever? He certainly will not do so, because he is concerned that another mark may never develop, and he will never become pure. And even if one does develop, what did the excision help him? He is afflicted as at first. Better for him to leave this one, and perhaps it will heal.
rashi:b7.1: With this blemish: it will not be permitted to him until another one develops in it.
rashi:b7.2: With this excision: since this excision does not help to purify him, he turns out to be impure forever, because we treat the mark as though it were still there. Who is to say that, had it been there, it would have healed?
rashi:b8.1: Did we learn yit’har: which implies that as soon as another mark develops in him, he becomes pure of the first.
rashi:b8.2: Or did we learn veyit’har: which implies that when another mark develops and he becomes pure of it, of the latter one, then he becomes pure of the first.
rashi:b9.1: For a bridegroom upon whom a leprous mark appeared: that the latter mark developed in him during the days of his wedding.
rashi:b9.2: What is the practical difference: even if we learned yit’har, he is impure because of the latter one until it heals; either way, impurity applies to him.
rashi:b10.1: They grant him: that the priest will not examine the mark, since as long as the priest has not seen it and declared him impure, he is not impure, for the Merciful One made it depend on the priest.
rashi:b10.2: For his cloak: his garment, if marks of garments developed in it.
rashi:b11.1: From the first he has become pure: as soon as this one developed, and of this one he is not impure, since we wait for him the days of the wedding, or of the Festival for anyone. But if we learned veyit’har, ultimately our waiting for him does not help him at all, since he is not pure of the first until the latter one heals.
rashi:b13.1: And dies: the one who slit it. What is the halakha with regard to penalizing his son after him, that he may never eat from that firstborn?
rashi:b14.1: If you say: in tractate Gittin, about one who sells his slave to a gentile, where we hold that we penalize him to redeem him for up to ten times his value, and there we raise the dilemma: if the seller died, what is the halakha with regard to penalizing his son after him? If you say, and resolve that we penalize there, that is the law there, since every day he removes him from mitzvot.
rashi:b15.1: And if you say: what we said in Mo’ed Katan (12b) about one who planned his labor for the Festival, who leaves his vineyard [unharvested] and says, “I will harvest it on the Festival, since it is a matter that would otherwise be lost, and the Sages permitted that on the Festival”: [there it is ruled that] it shall be lost and he shall not harvest it, since this is what he intended. And there we raise the dilemma: if he died before the Festival, what is the halakha with regard to penalizing his son after him, so that he may not harvest it on the Festival? And if you say [that they did not penalize the son], it is there that we do not penalize his son, since his father did not commit a prohibited act, as he died before the Festival.
rashi:b16.1: But here: he committed a prohibited act, as he caused a blemish in consecrated animals.
rashi:b16.2: On his property: on the firstborn.
rashi:b17.1: Whose thorns were removed: one took from it its thorns, which were detached and scattered over it.
rashi:b17.2: May be sown at the conclusion of the Sabbatical Year: since there is nothing to penalize, as he did not perform significant labor in the Sabbatical Year.
rashi:b17.3: Had been improved: it was fertilized with wagons and loads of manure.
rashi:b17.4: Had been enclosed: by means of a pen for animals, which are stood and bedded down in it for a month or two in order to fertilize it.
rashi:b17.5: It may not be sown: since we penalize him, as he performed significant labor in the Sabbatical Year.
tosafot:b2.1: Until it spreads over all of him: in all the texts it is written “or until his baheret shrinks to less than a split bean,” but in tractate Nega’im it is not there, as Rashi explained. And my teacher says that if we do read it, this is the meaning: he excised it and it became exactly a split bean, and of what remained part healed by itself, so that even if the part he excised were still there it would not be the size of a split bean.
tosafot:b11.1: From the first he has become pure; for the latter we wait the seven days of feasting: And if you say: but he still requires shaving and the birds, and is prohibited in marital relations all the days of his counting? One can say: for example, where he was only a quarantined leper. Alternatively, even a confirmed leper: granted that once he excised it he is impure by rabbinic law, he is nevertheless permitted to perform the shaving and the birds, to count his days of counting and to become pure by Torah law. But he cannot bring his atonement offerings, since he cannot put his hands into the Temple courtyard for the thumbs as long as he is impure by rabbinic law, as it says (Pesaḥim 92a): “Although a tevul yom does not enter otherwise, this one enters,” for they permitted it only for the Paschal offering.
tosafot:b13.1: Rabbi Yirmeya asked Rabbi Zeira: one who slits the ear of a firstborn and dies, do they penalize his son after him? In the chapter HaSholeaḥ (Gittin 44a) the Gemara poses first the dilemma of one who sells his slave, and in Mo’ed Katan, in the chapter Mi SheHafakh (12b), that of one who planned his labor; everywhere it says “if you say” from the other cases, and it resolves them all with “You learned it” from the field whose thorns were removed. My teacher says that he asked all three at once, and the Talmud set each one in the place where it belongs. Some texts in Mo’ed Katan (ibid.) read “Rava asked Rav Naḥman,” but most texts read Rabbi Yirmeya asking Rabbi Zeira, as here and in Gittin.
tosafot:b14.1: If you say: one who sells his slave to gentiles and dies, they penalized his son after him, since every day he removes him from mitzvot: One could still say that even if you say they did not penalize there, here they penalize, because there is a Torah prohibition; and so it is found in the chapter HaSholeaḥ, in the dilemma about one who sells his slave, and in Mo’ed Katan, in the dilemma about one who planned his labor on the Festival, where it says: “If you say they penalized one who slits, that is because there is a Torah prohibition.” In Gittin it could also have said: “If you say they did not penalize [one who slits], there they penalized because he removes him from mitzvot every day,” as with the slave. And in Mo’ed Katan too it gives one reason for one who slits and another for one who sells his slave, though it could have given one reason for both: “If you say they penalized one who slits and one who sells, because he committed a prohibited act; but one who planned his labor did not commit a prohibited act.”
tosafot:b17.1: That was cleared of thorns: Rashi explained that one took from it thorns that were detached and scattered over it, and he is right. One cannot say it refers to attached thorns, for then it could not be sown, since removing them is a Torah prohibition, as it improves the ground, as stated in Shabbat, in the chapter HaBoneh (103a), about one who plucks endives or trims shoots: in his own land he is liable for any amount, because of the improvement of the ground, even if he intends it for another purpose. So too here, there is improvement of the ground when he plucks thorns in order to plow for sowing. And so it is implied in the Jerusalem Talmud on the mishna: “There they are prohibited when its thorns were removed,” which implies that it explains [our case] as detached thorns.
tosafot:b17.2: Had been improved: in the Jerusalem Talmud it explains: what is improvement? Everyone plows once, and he plows twice.
tosafot:b17.3: If one improved it and died, his son may sow it: If this improvement is prohibited by rabbinic law, it is difficult: how does it resolve the case of one who slits the ear of a firstborn, which is by Torah law? And if it too is by Torah law, it is difficult in Gittin (44b), which resolves from it the case of the slave: let one say that it is different there, since it is more severe, as he removes him from mitzvot. One can say that he holds it is fitting to be more stringent with the Sabbatical Year than with all of them, as it says in Kiddushin (20a): How severe is even the dust of the Sabbatical Year.
gershom:b1.1: And it got excised: by itself.
gershom:b2.1: And the Rabbis say: he will never become pure until the second mark spreads over all of him, over his whole body, for then he is pure by Torah law, as it is written: “And if the leprosy… cover… from his head even to his feet” (Leviticus 13:12).
gershom:b3.1: Or until his baheret shrinks to less than a split bean: that is, if that first mark, which he excised intentionally, was not the size of a split bean, which is the Torah measure, he is pure immediately; and if it was the size of a split bean, he will not become pure until another mark develops in him and spreads over all of him. And Rabbi Eliezer holds that even though the one he excised was the size of a split bean, once another mark develops in him and he becomes pure of it, he becomes pure of the first as well, and it need not spread over all of him. Evidently Rabbi Eliezer does not penalize here, and the Rabbis do.
gershom:b4.1: With his property: with a firstborn he penalizes, since there is reason to say that he might come to cause a blemish in it either way. He thinks: if they permit it to me on account of that blemish, good; and if they do not, he thinks it is now no worse than before, since before it was forbidden to eat and now too it is forbidden. With his body, is there reason to say that he would come to excise it in the first place, either way? What “either way” is there here? If he excises it, perhaps another mark will develop, and when he becomes pure of it he will become pure of this one too; better for him not to excise this one and to wait until he becomes pure of it [by itself], than that he excise it and wait until another develops. Therefore Rabbi Eliezer does not penalize here, since another person would not come to excise it in the first place; but with his property, a firstborn, he penalizes.
gershom:b5.1: The Rabbis are not difficult in light of the Rabbis: for here they penalized him with what he did: he intended to permit it with this blemish, so the Rabbis penalized him by treating that blemish as though it were not there; but when another blemish develops in it, he may slaughter on account of that. And there they penalized him with what he did: he intended to excise it in order to purify himself, so the Rabbis penalized him, and it is as though it had not been excised; even when he becomes pure of the second mark we treat the first as though it were still there, and for that reason he does not become pure until it spreads over all of him.
gershom:b6.1: Did we learn yit’har: “When he will develop another leprous mark, he will become pure”; or did we learn veyit’har? Yit’har implies that when another mark develops in him and is healed, he becomes pure retroactively of the first, from the time of the excision; or did we learn veyit’har, which implies that only now, when he is healed of the second mark, does he become pure of the first, and not retroactively from the time of the excision.
gershom:b7.1: What is the practical difference: either way he will not become pure until he is healed of the second. The difference is for a bridegroom in whom another mark developed on his wedding day, that is, when the other mark developed he was a bridegroom; and to a bridegroom in whom a mark developed they grant the seven days of feasting and do not declare him impure, whether it developed on him or on his cloak or his garment, since we do not distress him all the days of his wedding, nor all the days of the Festival.
gershom:b8.1: If you say we learned yit’har: that he is pure retroactively from the time of the excision, that is, he is treated as one who was purified of the first before the second mark developed in him, then we grant him the seven days of feasting, since we consider it as though the mark developed in him only now and not before his wedding; for had it developed before his wedding, they would not grant him [the days]. And this is what it says: of the first impurity he has become pure; for the latter impurity we wait for him the seven days of feasting.
gershom:b9.1: And if you say we learned veyit’har: that is, he becomes pure of the first only now, when the second mark is healed. Ultimately, though you do not declare him impure on account of the latter, the one that developed during his wedding, for which you grant him the seven days of feasting, what does it help him? He remains impure from the first mark, since that impurity applies until the purification of the second mark, and he is impure even during the days of feasting.
gershom:b10.1: What? Did we learn yit’har or did we learn veyit’har? Let it stand.
gershom:b11.1: One who slits: we are dealing with either a priest or an Israelite: a priest with a certain firstborn, and an Israelite with an uncertain firstborn, which is eaten by him in its blemish. What is the halakha: do they penalize his son after him, so that it is forbidden to him to eat it? They penalized his son after him to redeem [the slave], since every day he removes him from mitzvot; but with a firstborn there is no such removal, and they did not penalize.
gershom:b12.1: Or if you say: one who planned his labor on the Festival, they did not penalize his son, etc., since labor on the intermediate days of the Festival is prohibited by rabbinic law and not by Torah law.
gershom:b13.1: Or perhaps they penalized his property, the firstborn, so that he may not eat it, not even his son.
gershom:b14.1: Whose thorns were removed: one uprooted the thorns from it.
gershom:b15.1: May be sown at the conclusion of the Sabbatical Year: since removing thorns is not considered labor.
gershom:b16.1: Had been improved: it was fertilized in the Sabbatical Year; or had been enclosed: he brought animals there to fertilize it in the Sabbatical Year. This is considered labor, being a subcategory of plowing; it may not be sown at the conclusion of the Sabbatical Year.
gershom:b17.1: If he improved it in the Sabbatical Year and died, his son may sow it at the conclusion of the Sabbatical Year.
